title: Paid on Time Means Paid Before the Penalty: Escrow Disbursement Under Reg X 1024.17(k) and 1024.34, and Where Servicers Actually Miss
summary: A mortgage servicer that escrows taxes and insurance has to pay each bill on or before the deadline to avoid a penalty, advance its own money when the account is short, and choose between installments and a lump sum by a rule most servicing teams have never read closely. The CFPB has found servicers sending payments that never arrived and leaving them unpaid for months. An account of the rule, the failure modes, and how our servicing agents read the bills and watch the dates.
body_markdown:
## Who This Is For


Heads of servicing, escrow and tax department managers, and servicing compliance officers at banks, independent servicers and subservicers. Also MSR owners who oversee a subservicer's escrow work and want to know which questions to ask.


## The Borrower Already Paid


An escrowed borrower has done their part. They paid a monthly amount that included taxes and insurance, and they reasonably expect the servicer to pay the county and the insurer. When a tax bill is paid late, the penalty lands on a borrower who paid on time. When an insurance premium is paid late, the policy can lapse, and the borrower may find out when the servicer force-places a more expensive policy on their home.


That is why the rule is strict. Section 6(g) of RESPA, at[12 U.S.C. 2605(g)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/12/2605) , requires a servicer to make escrow payments for taxes, insurance premiums and other charges in a timely manner as they become due. Regulation X turns that into specific obligations in two places.


## What the Rule Requires


[12 CFR 1024.34(a)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1024/34/) says a servicer that collects escrow for taxes, insurance or other charges must pay them on or before the deadline to avoid a penalty, as governed by 1024.17(k).[Section 1024.17(k)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1024/17/) is where the detail sits.


The servicer has to pay on time as long as the borrower's payment is not more than 30 days overdue. If the escrow account does not have enough money to cover the bill, the servicer has to advance its own funds to make the payment on time, and can then recover the advance through the escrow analysis. A discount for early payment is not a penalty, so missing a discount is not a violation, but missing the last day before a late charge is.


The installment rule in 1024.17(k)(3) is the one that surprises people. If a taxing jurisdiction offers a choice between paying annually and paying in installments, and it neither gives a discount for the annual payment nor charges a fee for installments, the servicer must pay in installments. Only if there is a discount for paying annually, or a fee for paying in installments, may the servicer choose the lump sum. A servicer that pays every county's full-year bill on the first due date, for operational simplicity, is collecting more escrow than it needs and is out of step with the rule in every jurisdiction that offers free installments.


For insurance, 1024.17(k)(5) adds a related constraint. A servicer may not force-place hazard insurance on a borrower with an escrow account for hazard insurance, whose payment is not more than 30 days overdue, unless it is unable to disburse funds from the escrow account to keep the borrower's policy in force. A lapsed policy caused by the servicer's own failure to pay is not a reason to force-place. Our post on[force-placed insurance](https://www.seiright.com/blog/force-placed-insurance-regulation-x-1024-37-ai-servicing) covers the notice sequence that follows when force-placement is actually allowed.


At payoff, 1024.34(b) requires the servicer to refund any remaining escrow balance within 20 days, excluding legal public holidays, Saturdays and Sundays, unless the borrower agrees to have it credited to a new loan with the same servicer. A failure on either the timely payment or the refund is a covered error under 1024.35(b)(4), so a borrower can send a notice of error and the servicer has to investigate and respond under the timelines our post on[Reg X notices of error](https://www.seiright.com/blog/reg-x-1024-35-notice-of-error-request-for-information-ai-mortgage-servicing) covers.


## What the CFPB Has Actually Found


The CFPB's[Supervisory Highlights Issue 33](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_supervisory-highlights_issue-33_2024-04.pdf) , the spring 2024 mortgage servicing edition, reported examiners finding servicers that failed to make timely disbursements from escrow accounts. In the cases described, payments the servicers sent never reached the taxing authorities or insurers, and the servicers did not reissue them for months. Borrowers incurred penalties, and the servicers covered those penalties only when borrowers complained.


The CFPB's 2019[consent order with Servis One, doing business as BSI Financial Services](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/enforcement/actions/servis-one-inc-db-bsi-financial-services/) , cited 1024.34(a) among its findings, tied to late tax and insurance payments.


Neither case involved a servicer deciding not to pay. Both are about payments that were scheduled, or believed sent, and then were not confirmed. That is the gap that matters operationally.


## Where Escrow Disbursement Goes Wrong


The misses cluster in a few places, and very few of them are in the payment system itself.


The bill is wrong or missing. Tax bills arrive from thousands of jurisdictions in thousands of formats, often through a tax service vendor, sometimes as a scanned image. A bill read with the wrong parcel number, the wrong installment due date, or a supplemental assessment that never made it into the escrow system produces a payment that is on time for the wrong amount, or no payment at all.


The due date is not the penalty date. Many jurisdictions have a due date and a later delinquency date, and the rule is written around the penalty. A servicer paying on the due date is safe. A servicer whose system holds the delinquency date and pays on it has no margin when a check takes a week to arrive.


The insurance renewal changed. A borrower switches carriers, or the carrier re-rates the policy after a claim, and the renewal premium the servicer pays is from last year's declarations page. The insurer applies a short payment and the policy lapses on the old carrier, or the new carrier was never paid at all.


The payment left and did not arrive. This is the CFPB's finding. A check that is not cashed within the usual window, or an electronic payment the payee does not confirm, needs someone to notice. Most escrow systems record that a disbursement was made. Fewer track whether it was received and applied.


The account was short and nobody advanced. When a tax bill comes in higher than projected, the escrow balance can be short on the due date. The rule says advance. A team working an exception queue in the last week before a delinquency date does not always see that the account is short until it is too late.


The loan moved. Disbursement calendars often break at a servicing transfer, and our post on[servicing transfers under 1024.33](https://www.seiright.com/blog/respa-servicing-transfer-reg-x-1024-33-ai-servicing-agent) covers the period where both the old and new servicer believe the other one is paying.


## How Our Servicing Agents Watch the Dates


Our[Escrow Manager](https://www.seiright.com/for-servicers/escrow-manager) starts with the documents. It reads the tax bills and insurance declarations behind each escrowed loan, including the ones that arrive as images, and writes each one into the[Loan Graph](https://www.seiright.com/platform/loan-graph) with the parcel or policy number, amount, installment schedule, due date and penalty date, cited to the page. When a bill disagrees with what the escrow system expects, a different amount, a new installment, a carrier the servicer has never paid, it stops and goes to the escrow team as a named exception with the bill and the figure it expected.


From the bills, it builds the disbursement calendar the rule needs. For each item it records the deadline to avoid a penalty, whether the jurisdiction offers a discount for annual payment or charges for installments, and therefore whether 1024.17(k)(3) requires installments or allows the lump sum. The[Rulebook](https://www.seiright.com/how-it-works#rulebook) holds those jurisdiction-level facts with their source, so the reason a servicer paid annually in one county and in installments in the next is written down.


Then it watches what the payment system does. Ahead of each penalty date, it checks that a disbursement is scheduled for the right amount, and flags an account where the balance will be short so someone can approve the advance. After the payment, where the servicer connects its tax service's paid-status data or the insurer's confirmations, it looks for evidence that the payee received and applied it, and an item still unconfirmed after a set number of days becomes an exception with the payee, the amount, the date sent and the penalty date. That last check is the one the CFPB's findings point to, because a payment nobody confirmed is the one nobody reissues.


The agent does not send money. Disbursement and advances stay in the servicer's payment system under its own approvals. And it does not decide whether a borrower is reimbursed for a penalty the servicer caused. Under 1024.35, that is the servicer's correction to make, and the agent's part is to hand the escrow team the bill, the date it should have been paid, the date it was paid, and the penalty that resulted. Every step runs through[Triple Check](https://www.seiright.com/how-it-works#triple-check) , and the[Evidence Trail](https://www.seiright.com/how-it-works#evidence-trail) keeps the calendar and each confirmation, so an examiner sampling escrowed loans can see when each bill was due and when it was paid.


## The Questions Worth Asking Your Escrow Team


For a servicing head or an MSR owner reviewing a subservicer, a handful of questions show whether the operation meets the rule or only intends to. Does the disbursement calendar hold the penalty date or the due date? How does the team decide between installments and lump sum, and is that decision recorded per jurisdiction? What happens to a payment that has not been confirmed received after 30 days? How many advances were made last year, and how many penalties did the servicer reimburse? The last number is the one that tells you whether the controls work, because every reimbursed penalty is a late payment someone found after the fact.


The borrower's view is simpler. They paid. The county and the insurer should have been paid too, before the penalty, and the servicer should be able to show that it happened.
